facts.claim: 'Killer + The Sound' is a mashup of Phoebe Bridgers' 'Killer' and Noah Gundersen's 'The Sound', recorded together as one performance.
The stripped-down video and track were recorded at Seattle's Studio X, with Abby Gundersen on piano and vocals.
'The Sound' comes from Gundersen's album White Noise. 'Killer' comes from Bridgers' 2017 debut album Stranger in the Alps (Dead Oceans).
Noah Gundersen said it was recorded on the last day of the tour he and Bridgers did together, in a few spare afternoon hours.
Gundersen said he was a big fan of Bridgers' work, had listened to her record obsessively, and wanted to make something with her.
Bridgers said she had been a fanatic Noah Gundersen fan since her teens, and that he made her more comfortable being honest in her songs.
The single was released in April 2018 through Dead Oceans (catalog DOC172dig1) as a standalone, non-album single. It runs 7:55.
The official video was directed by Ben Park. The performance video credits Park as camera and editor.
A fan wiki lists the songwriters as Phoebe Bridgers, Noah Gundersen and Abby Gundersen, and the producer as Andy D. Park.
Bridgers was born in 1994 in Pasadena, California, and released 'Killer' as her debut 7" in 2015 on Ryan Adams' Pax AM label.

research.lineage: It sits in the Seattle/Los Angeles indie-folk and singer-songwriter tradition, a stripped-down live collaboration between two confessional songwriters.

draft:
The tenderest request in **Killer + The Sound** is a mercy killing. "I hope you kiss my rotten head / And pull the plug," the narrator asks, picturing a body kept alive by a machine and asking the person they love to end it gently. It's a strange way to say forever. It's also exactly how this song loves: through dark jokes, worst-case scenarios, and a refusal to look away.

The first half is Phoebe Bridgers' "Killer," a song she first put out in 2015 and later included on her 2017 debut *Stranger in the Alps*. Its narrator builds a scary self-image and then can't live up to it. They spook a partner by talking about Dahmer on the couch and call themselves a killer, but they can't stand the thought of sleeping next to a body. In the same breath they admit they'd fake sleep just to count the other person's breathing. The menace is a pose, and the pose keeps slipping. A chorus that starts out hungry for blood comes back confessing it's helplessly in love, and nothing in the song settles which one is true.

Then the song turns into Noah Gundersen's "The Sound," from his album *White Noise*, and the voice turns outward and gets sharper. Its "you" is a burnout picking fights with strangers, coasting on other people's forgiveness, holding on to a Johnny Cash middle finger long after it stopped meaning anything. The chant gets blunt: "shut up and listen." Coming after "Killer," it plays like an answer. One half admits how frightening it is to love someone that much, and the other is fed up with someone who won't take the love on offer. Exasperation and devotion sit right next to each other.

The sound stays modest. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through slow arpeggios. A breathy, close-miked voice with a slight vibrato leads, and a second voice comes in to harmonize tightly. The room sounds small and dry, with nothing smoothed over. Abby Gundersen played piano and sang. They cut it at Seattle's Studio X in a few spare afternoon hours on the last day of a tour Bridgers and Gundersen played together. That backstory explains the mood. Gundersen said he'd listened to her record obsessively. Bridgers said she'd been a fanatic fan of his since her teens, and that he made her more comfortable being honest in her songs. So this is two confessional writers from the Seattle and Los Angeles folk scenes trading songs as a thank-you to each other.

It sticks because it hands you both sides of loving someone hard, the fear of what you'd do for them and the anger at what they won't do for themselves, and lets them harmonize instead of argue.

factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly, and it is two consecutive lines.

factCheck.note: Rests on the lyrics 'When a machine keeps me alive' and 'pull the plug'. The mercy-killing framing is interpretation.
